learn.hook: Can you lose a match and still be the hero of the day? This story says yes!
points: 'Change of Heart' is a sports story about how a person's feelings and choices can change.
A 'change of heart' is an idiom meaning a change in one's opinion or feelings, usually towards something kinder.
Sports stories have a goal (winning), a conflict (a tough opponent or a hard choice) and a turning point.
Kabaddi is a team sport from India in which a 'raider' enters the other half and tries to tag opponents while saying 'kabaddi, kabaddi'.
When reading, note how a character's thoughts at the start differ from their actions at the end.

example.q: Read: Sana wanted to win the kabaddi final at any cost. Late in the match, the rival captain, Divya, slipped and twisted her ankle. "Keep going! Now we'll win easily!" shouted Sana's teammates. But when Sana saw Divya wince in pain, she had a change of heart. She stopped, helped Divya up and called for the first-aid kit. Sana's team lost by two points, yet the whole crowd clapped for her. What was Sana's change of heart?
steps: At the start she wanted to win 'at any cost'.
When Divya got hurt, her teammates wanted to keep playing.
Sana saw Divya's pain and stopped to help her.
example.answer: She stopped caring only about winning and helped her injured rival instead.

learn.reallife: Some real athletes have stopped to help a fallen rival in races — and crowds remember those moments longer than the results.

quiz.q: In the story, who was Divya?
quiz.explain: The passage calls Divya 'the rival captain'.
quiz.mistake: Does not read the description of the character

quiz.q: At the start, what did Sana want?
options: to win the final at any cost
quiz.explain: The first line says she wanted to win 'at any cost'.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the start and the end of the story

quiz.q: In the story, "Sana saw Divya wince in pain". 'Wince' means to:
options: make a quick face because of pain
quiz.explain: To wince is to make a sudden face showing pain.
quiz.mistake: Guesses without using the clue 'in pain'

quiz.q: What did Sana's teammates want to do when Divya got hurt?
quiz.explain: They shouted, 'Keep going! Now we'll win easily!'
quiz.mistake: Confuses the teammates' reaction with Sana's

quiz.q: What does 'a change of heart' mean in the story?
options: Sana moved to a new school
Sana changed her feelings and decided to be kind
quiz.explain: It is an idiom for changing one's opinion or feelings.
quiz.mistake: Takes the idiom literally

quiz.q: Why did the crowd clap for Sana even though her team lost?
options: She showed kindness and good sportsmanship
quiz.explain: The crowd admired her for helping an injured rival.
quiz.mistake: Thinks people only cheer for winners

quiz.q: What is the turning point of the story?
options: Sana sees Divya in pain and stops to help
The crowd claps at the end
quiz.explain: The turning point is when Sana's feelings and actions change.
quiz.mistake: Confuses the turning point with the ending

quiz.q: Which word best describes Sana at the end?
quiz.explain: Compassionate means caring about others' suffering — like helping Divya.
quiz.mistake: Judges her only by the lost match

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Sana's team lost! So why is she the hero of the story?'
teach.praise: Tweet! Sana had a change of heart and helped her hurt rival. Being kind is the biggest win!
teach.nudge: What did Sana do when Divya got hurt?

learn.hook: The scoreboard shows who won the game. Sportsmanship shows who won respect.
points: Sportsmanship means playing fairly, following the rules, respecting opponents and accepting results gracefully.
A 'good sport' wins without boasting and loses without sulking.
Useful words: fair play, opponent (the person you play against), teammate, referee/umpire, gracious, honour.
Opposites: win ↔ lose, victory ↔ defeat, fair ↔ unfair, teammate ↔ opponent.
Shaking hands after a match, cheering good play by the other side and accepting the umpire's decision are signs of sportsmanship.

example.q: Think it through: In a cricket match, Kiran knows the ball touched his bat before the catch, but the umpire did not see it. He walks off the field anyway. What does this show?
steps: Kiran could have stayed because the umpire missed it.
He chose honesty over his own score.
Being honest and fair in sport is sportsmanship.
example.answer: It shows honesty and good sportsmanship.

learn.reallife: At the end of every match, players shake hands — a small habit that shows respect, whoever wins.

games.title: Good sport or bad sport?
items: clapping for the other team's good shot

quiz.q: What is sportsmanship?
options: Playing fairly and respecting others, whether you win or lose
quiz.explain: Sportsmanship is about fairness and respect, not just winning.
quiz.mistake: Thinks sportsmanship means winning

quiz.q: What is an 'opponent'?
options: a member of your own team
quiz.explain: Your opponent is on the other side in a game.
quiz.mistake: Confuses opponent with teammate

quiz.q: What is the opposite of 'victory'?
quiz.explain: Victory means winning; defeat means losing.
quiz.mistake: Picks a synonym instead of an antonym

quiz.q: Which action shows good sportsmanship?
options: Shaking hands with the winning team after losing
Refusing to talk to the other team
quiz.explain: Congratulating the winners shows respect.
quiz.mistake: Thinks showing anger is acceptable after losing

quiz.q: A 'good sport' is someone who:
options: is very good at all sports
quiz.explain: 'A good sport' is an idiom for someone fair and gracious.
quiz.mistake: Takes the phrase literally

quiz.q: 'Fair play' means:
options: playing only when the weather is fair
playing honestly and by the rules
quiz.explain: Fair play means following the rules honestly.
quiz.mistake: Takes 'fair' in a different meaning

quiz.q: The umpire gives a decision you don't agree with. What is the sporting thing to do?
options: Walk off and stop the game
quiz.explain: Respecting the umpire's decision is part of sportsmanship.
quiz.mistake: Thinks arguing is the right way to disagree

quiz.q: Which word means 'kind and polite, even in defeat'?
quiz.explain: A gracious person stays polite and kind.
quiz.mistake: Does not know the meaning of 'gracious'

teach.ask: Gappu is cross: 'I lost the flying race! Should I sulk in my nest all day?'
teach.praise: Tweet! A good sport plays fair and respects others, win or lose. I'll go congratulate the winner!
teach.nudge: What should a good sport do after losing?

topics.title: Adverbs: how, when, where, how often

learn.hook: Sana ran FAST, helped KINDLY and played FAIRLY. Those capital words are adverbs — let's meet them!
points: An adverb tells us more about a verb (and sometimes an adjective or another adverb).
Adverbs of manner tell how: quickly, bravely, kindly, carefully. Many are made by adding -ly to adjectives (quick → quickly).
Adverbs of time tell when (now, soon, yesterday); of place tell where (here, there, outside); of frequency tell how often (always, often, sometimes, never).
Some adverbs don't end in -ly: fast, hard, well, late. 'Good' is an adjective; its adverb is 'well' (She plays well).
Careful: 'hardly' means 'almost not'. 'He worked hard' is very different from 'He hardly worked'!

example.q: Think it through: Find the adverbs and what they tell us: 'Yesterday, Sana played bravely outside.'

learn.reallife: Sports commentary is full of adverbs: 'He bowled quickly', 'She always smiles', 'They played well today.'

items.text: Please walk ___ on the wet floor.
Our team ___ gives up; we keep trying.

quiz.q: Which word is an adverb in: 'The raider moved swiftly'?
quiz.explain: 'Swiftly' tells how the raider moved.
quiz.mistake: Confuses the verb with the adverb

quiz.q: What is the adverb form of 'happy'?
quiz.explain: Change y to i and add -ly: happily.
quiz.mistake: Forgets to change y to i

quiz.q: Which sentence uses the right adverb?
quiz.explain: 'Well' is the adverb; 'good' is an adjective.
quiz.mistake: Uses the adjective 'good' as an adverb

quiz.q: In 'We often play kabaddi after school', 'often' is an adverb of:
quiz.explain: 'Often' tells how often we play.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up kinds of adverbs

quiz.q: Which is an adverb of place?
quiz.explain: 'Outside' tells where. 'Slowly' is manner, 'tomorrow' is time, 'sometimes' is frequency.
quiz.mistake: Does not classify adverbs correctly

quiz.q: 'He hardly practised before the match.' This means he:
quiz.explain: 'Hardly' means almost not.
quiz.mistake: Thinks 'hardly' means 'with great effort'

quiz.q: Fill in: 'The match will start ___.'
quiz.explain: 'Soon' is an adverb of time telling when the match starts.
quiz.mistake: Uses an adjective in place of an adverb

quiz.q: Which adverb does NOT end in -ly?
quiz.explain: 'Fast' is both an adjective and an adverb; it does not take -ly.
quiz.mistake: Thinks all adverbs end in -ly

teach.ask: Gappu chirps: 'I fly quickly, I sing sweetly, I sleep soundly! What are all these -ly words?'
teach.praise: Tweet! Adverbs tell how, when, where or how often an action happens. I learned it happily!
teach.nudge: Which word does an adverb usually tell us more about?
